title: Structured output and tool use
summary: How to get data your code can trust out of a model with JSON schemas, and how tool use lets the model ask your code to look things up or act.
youWillLearn: Why parsing free text from a model breaks, and how a JSON schema fixes it
Why a valid shape still needs checking before it reaches your database
How tool use works: the model asks, your code runs, the model answers
Why the model must never decide whose data a tool touches

glossary.structured output: Asking the API for an answer that must match a schema you define, so your code gets clean data instead of prose.
glossary.JSON schema: A description of the shape JSON must have: which fields, which types, which are required.
glossary.Zod: A popular TypeScript library for describing data shapes once and using them for both types and runtime checks.
glossary.tool use: Also called function calling: you describe functions to the model, and it can reply with a request to call one, with arguments.
glossary.tool_use: The content block a model returns when it wants a tool called: the tool's name, an id, and the input arguments.
glossary.tool_result: The content block you send back with the output of a tool call, matched to the request by its id.
glossary.RLS: Row Level Security: Postgres rules that decide which rows each logged-in user may read or change, enforced by the database itself.

steps.title: "Sure! Here are your tasks:"
body: Maya wants Notely to pull to-dos out of a note into her task list. Claude Code wrote a prompt that says "Return the tasks as JSON", then calls JSON.parse on the reply.
Nine times in ten it works. The tenth reply starts with "Sure! Here are your tasks:", or wraps the JSON in a code fence, and the parse throws. Free text is for people, not for code.

scene.caption: The model replies in friendly prose. The server's JSON parser chokes on it.

steps.title: Hand the model a form to fill in
body: Instead of asking nicely, give the API a JSON schema: the exact fields, their types, which ones are required.

With structured output turned on, the API constrains the answer to that shape. No greeting, no code fence, no missing bracket. Whenever the answer finishes normally, your code receives data it can parse.

callout.text: Asking a guest to "write down your details" on a blank page versus handing them a form with labeled boxes. Same person, far more usable result.

scene.caption: The schema rides along with the request. The answer comes back in exactly that shape.

steps.title: One schema for types and the API
body: In TypeScript, Zod lets you describe the shape once. The SDK turns it into a JSON schema for the request, and checks the reply against it.
You get back parsed_output: a typed object, not a string. Your editor knows tasks[0].title exists before you run anything.

code.caption: zodOutputFormat comes from @anthropic-ai/sdk/helpers/zod. A cut-off or refused answer will not fit the schema, so check stop_reason first.

scene.caption: One Zod schema becomes the JSON schema and the TypeScript type.

steps.title: Right shape, wrong facts
body: A schema guarantees the shape, not the truth. The due date can be a valid string for a day that does not exist in the note. A task can be invented.
So check the content before it reaches the database: is the date real and in the future, is the title non-empty, did we already save this task? Then insert, as the logged-in user.

callout.text: Keep schemas small and flat. Prefer null for "unknown" over a guessed value, and say so in the field's description.

scene.caption: Shape is guaranteed. Content still gets checked before it is saved.

steps.title: Tools: the model asks, your code acts
body: Now Notely gets a chat. Maya asks: "When is the logo due?" The model does not have her notes. It needs to look.

With tool use, you describe functions it may request, like search_notes. Instead of an answer, the model can reply: "please call search_notes with query 'logo deadline'". Your code runs it. The model never touches your database itself.

scene.caption: The model gets a list of tools it may ask for. It replies with a request, not an answer.

steps.title: The round trip, step by step
body: 1. You send the question plus tool definitions. 2. The reply has stop_reason: "tool_use" and a tool_use block. 3. Your code runs the function. 4. You send the output back as a tool_result with the same id. 5. The model writes the final answer.
Two calls to the model, one to your database. Remember: the API has no memory, so call two re-sends the whole conversation.

code.caption: The id links the result to the request. Then the model answers: "Friday."

scene.caption: Your code runs the search and hands the result back. Then the model can answer.

steps.title: Defining Notely's search tool
body: A tool is a name, a description and an input schema. The description is a prompt: it tells the model when to use the tool, so write it like one.
strict: true makes the API hold the arguments to the schema exactly. Notice what is missing from the inputs: any user id. The route already knows who is logged in.

code.caption: Lesson 5 shows how search_notes finds notes by meaning, not only by keyword.

scene.caption: The tool definition: a name, a description that says when to use it, and an input schema.

steps.title: The model must not pick whose data
body: Tool arguments come from the model, and the model reads user text. If search_notes took a user_id argument, a crafted message could ask for someone else's notes.

So: take identity from the session, never from tool input. Run queries as the logged-in user, so RLS limits the rows. Validate every argument. For tools that change or delete things, ask the user to confirm first.

callout.text: Read every tool's input_schema. Any user_id, email or table name in there? Does the handler use the service role key, which skips RLS? Are tool errors returned as a tool_result with is_error: true instead of crashing the route? Does anything destructive run without a confirm?

scene.caption: If the model could choose the user id, a crafted message could read anyone's notes.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: When code needs the answer, ask for structured output against a schema, then check the content before saving it.

When the model needs to look something up or act, give it tools. It replies with a request; your code decides, runs it with the logged-in user's identity, and sends back the result. The model asks. Your code is in charge.

quiz.question: Claude Code extracts tasks with "Return JSON only" in the prompt and JSON.parse on the reply. It fails now and then. What is the sturdier fix?

options.text: Add "ONLY JSON, NO OTHER TEXT" in capitals.
options.why: That lowers the failure rate but cannot guarantee it. A schema-constrained answer can.

options.text: Strip everything before the first { with a regex.
options.why: That patches one failure style and misses others, like truncated or slightly malformed JSON.

options.text: Use structured output with a schema, and read parsed_output.
options.why: The API constrains the answer to the schema, so every completed answer parses into the right shape. Prompt wording alone cannot promise that.

quiz.question: In tool use, who actually runs search_notes?

options.text: Your server code, after the model asks for it.
options.why: The model only returns a tool_use request. Your code decides whether to run it, runs it, and returns a tool_result.

options.text: The model, by connecting to your database.
options.why: The model has no access to your systems. It can only ask your code to do things.

options.text: The provider's servers, using your database password.
options.why: For tools you define, the provider never runs anything on your behalf. You hold the keys and run the code.

quiz.question: A tool Claude Code wrote is get_notes(user_id), and the handler uses the service role key. What is the risk?

options.text: None, because the model is told to use the current user's id.
options.why: Instructions can be overridden by crafted input. Security cannot depend on the model following the rules.

options.text: Crafted text can make the model request another user's id, and nothing in the database stops it.
options.why: The model picks the argument and the service role skips RLS. Take the user from the session and query as that user.

options.text: It is slower, because each call carries a user id.
options.why: Speed is not the problem. Letting model output choose whose data to read is.

takeaways: Code needs data, not prose. Use structured output with a schema instead of parsing free text.
A schema guarantees shape, not truth. Check dates, duplicates and content before you save.
With tool use, the model only asks. Your code runs the tool and returns a tool_result.
Write tool descriptions like prompts: say when to use the tool.
Never let tool arguments choose identity. Take the user from the session and let RLS limit the rows.
